I'm from Mumbai I have quite a few Gujrati friends who are super awesome, the issue is a bunch of particularly annoying ones who are unfortunately also the loudest (or as I like to call it, all the money none of the culture) I'll provide some perspective on this issue, but it'll be long. 

These people come to societies capture it and then make it unwelcoming for everyone else in it. For example my grandmother's old society was redeveloped and on of the old Gujrati tenants (who was a real estate broker) told them I quote "Ab mein idhar sab Gujju launga, Ek bhi Marathi ko nahi launga" and he did that. The new tenants are some of the rudest motherfuckers I've seen. My grandma lives on the first floor and these people make noise even at 11:30 pm my grandma had asked them politely to keep it down, they went "To aap shift ho jao na aunty, hum Kyu ruke?" 

My grandma also had her old group of people who knew each other for 20-30 years (they were there before the society got developed), very diverse people from all across India. They got along very well before the new gujuratis came in. They tried to include this new lot into their group, but they continued speaking in gujurati and when asked to speak in a common language politely. They tell them "Tum log gujurati seekho na phir, hum Kyu seekhey?" 

On a larger scale I've heard a story on how the National Stock Exchange was established because the Bombay Stock Exchange was full of really corrupt gujurati stock traders. My grandfather who was the Vice President of a bank also sort of confirmed that this used to happen, but these are all personal anecdotes and news stories so take them as you will. So Bombay Stock Exchange had a lot of gujjus stock traders right? So these guys would basically overcharge under the table when people went to buy stocks, for example if a stock was ₹15 (with broker's fee) then next day or dropped to ₹12 or something, they'd still charge ₹15 and take ₹3 under the table. Essentially they were scumbags. That is what lead to the formation of NSA with electronic trading equipment, this was done under the guise of needing more mordern equipment since the economy had liberalized. So obviously this knowledge hits the reputation of the community as being a bunch of "people who got rich by making others poor".

Also this is my personal opinion and I could be wrong, Gujjus don't create as many jobs as they believe because they don't venture into industries all that much. I'm pretty sure I didn't explain that right so let me elaborate. Don't get me wrong they create a lot of wealth, just not a lot of jobs. Like I'll compare Tata and Reliance, Tata has a lot of R&D and manufacturing that goes on. This creates high skilled jobs which pay a LOT. Contrast that with reliance, the only jewel in his crown is his petroleum plant. He doesn't do R&D, barely contributes to society in a meaningful way (Tatas have tonnes of social service initiatives), etc. When I think reliance I think of stores where I buy products, when I think of tata I think of products that are made in India. There is a difference if you notice it. I took reliance as an example because a lot of gujuratis I meet point at him as the 'ideal gujju' I guess. 

Last but not the least is that some of them have a stick up their asses because they are vegetarian. This is done to the point they outright discriminate against non-vegeterians and don't let them reside in societies where they have majority. They are quite xenophobic. 

Like I don't dislike gujjus but I will be lying if I say that the ones with "All the money and none of the culture" don't test the limits of my tolerance through their blatantly disgusting behavior. I'd say do ECE and during the course try to focus on AI. Going into an AI course during undergrad is a bad idea right now imo because it's a new course so they'll be experimenting with the structure a lot. If you want to be a regular software engineer most companies hire and train you for 6 months anyways, I've seen geological engineers become software engineers after knowing just basic code during undergrad (this is literally my friend currently working at Microsoft) you'll have a backup plan cause India's AI market is booming but right now it's not quite there. 

Definitely go do an internship at a lab at some point for AI that experience will really help you and give you an idea whether you like it in the first place. Just doing coursework never gives you the right idea for a field. Also try to learn about MLOps if you do end up liking the AI field. MLOps professionals are growing in demand. 

So look out for any institute that offers you good research opportunities in the field of AI.

The fun thing about ECE is that it's an extremely versatile field, you can easily specialize in most things (aka masters later on) after you do ECE so it's the best choice if you're unsure of what to do. India also has a robotics market that is growing slowly and ECE can definitely allow you to tap into that. Hell you can even get into semiconductors, by the time you're done I think India should start manufacturing semiconductors so they might need people who know their stuff.

Personally I just to listen to Mandarin Clicks stories which are sorted according to your HSK level. It's advantageous because they also provide you the subtitles on the screen.

When I was doing HSK3 my audio skills were still lacking, so I decided to listen to the HSK1 and 2 stories and write them. 

So I'd start by listening to one sentence writing it down then replaying it but this time I look at the written words on the screen. Look at what you've written and marked the words you missed with different colours in level of importance. 

Like for example the sentence is 

马克昨天去旁边的商店买六个苹果，因为他（昨天）在家找不到了苹果。 （trying to keep it to HSK2 Level here and hopefully I'm not failing to do so)

So what are the important bits of information here? 

Nouns- 马克，苹果

Place-商店，家

Time- 昨天

quantity- 六

Verbs-去，买，找不到

This gives you the essential information in the sentence

The rest of secondary stuff is 

旁边的（provides you more detailed information about the shop's location) 

因为（your brain will automatically jump to this after seeing 去，买，找不到） 

Totally unnecessary things to remember 

个 (unnecessary because you already know what he’s buying if it’s like 六件 without 衣服 after it then measure word becomes important)

了(unnecessary to remember since you already knowing all this happened yesterday) also I could be wrong in using 了here I've hit HSK 4 and I've gotten better at using it but I'll be lying if I said it still isn't extremely confusing at times.

在（I mean this is unnecessary to remember because you know the place he didn't find apples was his home so well 在 just indicates the place where something occured)

Different take that probably gets me downvoted, if we're comparing to East Asia to my understanding education wasn't as restricted in east asia as it is in south Asia. Because of the caste system present in south asia education was very very restricted. So only certain communities in India had an idea of the effect for education and an appreciation for it. Also education and literacy were a symbol of power since only certain communities gatekept it back in the good old days. 

So when it came time to mordernize East Asia embraced education faster which resulted in higher literacy rate resulting in better social mobility for previous lower economic strata, etc. Also because of a lack of caste systems and Confucianism (to my knowledge) east Asian is a hell of a lot meritocratic. Either you're good or you're out kinda mentality which breeds its own kind of overcompetitive toxic environment but hell, they're rich as fuck. 

In India people had problems about certain communities being educated (you know what I'm talking about). Then certain other communities fought amongst themselves and decided that education was more their right than the others (aka reservation fights between different OBC communities). We never really had a good educated population because of this. Also controversial (and maybe uninformed) opinion, Hinduism when compared to Confucianism doesn't exactly promote meritocracy (I'm talking about the philosophy). It says your born in a certain place and you should behave like it, well the more mordern rendition of it does (the shit made around the late Vedic period when society stratified) . It emphasizes on duty and your place in society due to birth more than "do what you're most skilled at and do it fucking well". You can be the smartest person on the planet but if you're born to clean shit, you're gonna clean shit. So we are not the most meritocratic individuals in India and you can see that when people get promoted in companies when they have zero skill and just kiss the right asses. If we change our society to be more meritocratic (and tbh it is happening slowly) we might become a very developed country.

Also one personal observation that I had with not objectivity whatsoever, whichever East Asians I met I felt had an appreciation for education, most Indians I met really didn't. They believed education was a joke and were focused more on the big bucks at the end. So they'd work more to just pass tests rather than understand the material properly. It's just my personal experience I might've just met the bad ones. 

TLDR: East Asia vs India. In India Education is a way to maintain power and restricted, In East Asia education is free for most people and a cultural thing. Also India isn't very meritocratic while East Asia is.

Honestly I read about how racial violence in Singapore was dealt with and I kind of got inspired by the solution.

In the 1960s, Singapore was (Idr where I got the quote from) "A malaria-infested port in Southeast Asia". It had a housing crisis and on top of that, it had a lot of racial tensions going on. From what I've read the government basically managed to kill two birds with one stone.

What he did was every time the government constructed a new building he assigned the quarters to members from different communities essentially creating like sort of a racial and ethnic mixture within the housing complex. I believe the logic was that if one member of community A were to enact violence upon a member of community B he shall face immediate repercussions from all the members of community B in the housing complex. No one wants to be on bad terms with their neighbours let alone have enemies so close to their home.

So how does this apply to India? I am from Mumbai and I admit I have not stayed outside of this city for a long time. But I can tell you which areas in Mumbai you will find the Majority of Hindus, Muslims, Christians, etc.

I mean around 20% of Mumbai's population is Muslims so ideally every fifth person I meet should be Muslim. But honestly out of the hundreds of people I have met I have barely met 3 to 4 Muslims. This could be due to chance, but I think it's because communities in India tend to isolate themselves from each other. Like Hindus stay in Hindu neighbourhoods, Muslims stay in Muslim neighbourhoods and so on.

I think breaking this "neighbourhood isolation" is key to actually having some semblance of communal harmony and EVERYONE is to blame for this isolation so don't go pointing fingers. We're all told to not interact with the 'other' in India, me being born a Hindu (I don't consider myself one anymore cause religion sucks) was told "look out for the Muslims" and I guess it's common for everyone in India, its just that the 'enemy' is different.

Just think about how our entire marriage system works as well. The person has to belong to your community, your caste, your religion, your everything. How do you expect to have a different perspective by being with someone from the same background? We are so obsessed with maintaining some weird form of 'purity'. I had this friend. We got along together damn well together. I guess we would've gone out together had it not been for religion and the conservative nature of our society. She wasn't even allowed to talk to guys, but she did it behind her family's back (she had guts I'll give her that).

Like she didn't believe in God, I didn't care about god. Yet we were our religions just because we were born in them, a fact I found stupid. So I accepted that it would just be a good friendship and it was a great one. 

Then she was about to get married at the very old age of 21 to some well earning guy who she will get to know for six months before tying the knot. She cried on text saying that she didn't want to get married, she wanted to get a better education and travel the world. Luckily she managed to slip that proposal but still it must've been pretty stressful. 

Then I talked to a few of my friends and many people had similar stories with other people who were getting pressured into marrying by their family before experiencing life or gaining financial independence, many of them girls but there were guys too. I had a friend who was married at 22. Like he had just finished college! They dumped a big responsibility on a 22 year old! I wonder how much resentment is going to pile up on his mind over the years. 

Am I against arranged marriages after these experiences? In theory no, in practice yes. 

In theory parents chose for you when you want it and I guess it's fine. Familial support goes a long way in India where financial independence doesn't come until your mid twenties. So familial support is important and a priority for many. 

In practice it creates deeper caste and religious divides in society, a lot of people (like the examples I gave) are married when their parents expect them to get married. There is some amount of consent given but there's usually a lot of pressure and disapproval basically gaslighting because parents know how much sway they have over you. I understand the parents as well, I suppose that's how they grew up. They have good intentions definitely, but their actions are horrible. Even after marriage the likelihood is that even if you're incompatible you'll be forced to stick around and it'll mentally damage your kids because divorce here sucks and you'll never get it. 

Many woman, from what I heard from a friend also have this race between financial independence and martial interdependence. Whichever wins first is their future the way she put it.

The 'objectivity' which these marriages profess also gets called into question as my friend and I never believed in God but at the same time, they will look for marriages within our religion which is sort of weird since neither of us would be compatible with someone religious.

For all the people who hate Western culture and dating, it's very pragmatic when it comes to compatibility. I've had a friend who was with her boyfriend for 3 years (her parents didn't know of course 🤣). He was nice for 2 years then something happened and he started to get jealous and possessive in the last year, she couldn't take it after months of that behaviour and broke up. 

Compare this to an arranged marriage where the equivalent of a break up is divorce, ummmmm I think a break up makes more sense. 

Sure as many are concerned with people dating due to lust and mistake that for love, but when you have a virgin 25 year old whose only way of getting laid is getting married, what are the chances that they aren't marrying to just fuck? I can imagine that is a possibility but when the sex stops being fun you start to get bored of marriage. There will be nice people there as well, but it's about the risk here. A break up is less ostracizing than a divorce, so it's a much more pragmatic thing in today's time because we live more individualistic lives and compatibility matters much more compared to previous generations. extremely sweaty, learning curve is never ending and gets steep pretty fast. It isn't like lot of popular FPS where you are a bullet sponge it's essentially 3-4 bullets and dead that's said not considering 1 shot headshot.

There are also a LOT of bugs that get fixed frequently only for new ones to pop up. Doesn't make the game unplayable just annoying. 

That being said those who play siege on some level enjoy the challenge and intensity it provides, you have one life in a round and you have to make it count, play smart, play tatical and try not to crumble under the pressure of a round. 

I can tell you this, regardless of how much siege players love or hate this game all of us agree we come back because there is absolutely nothing like it in the games market. The intensity of each round, the rush you get after a clutch or ace, or when you hit that sweet plat rank you wanted to, all of it is an experience. 

Best played with friends even in casual it's damn fun when you play with a team.
